title: 48 Hours on a Glacier Shooting My Biggest Campaign Yet
creator: Tomas Lindqvist
description:
Behind the scenes of a two-day commercial shoot in Iceland, from the gear I packed to the shots that almost didn't happen.

Gear in this video:
Camera body and two primes, a cheap tripod I keep breaking, and way too many batteries.

Music by my friend Elin.

0:00 Landing in Reykjavik
1:10 The brief
2:20 Day one on the ice
3:40 What went wrong

sentences.t: Okay, it is five in the morning, I have had zero coffee, and we just landed in Reykjavik.
So this one is a bit different from my normal videos.
Usually I am out here shooting landscapes for myself, just me and a tripod and a lot of complaining.
But this week I am actually on a job.
A few months ago I got an email from Halvard Outfitters, the Norwegian jacket company, asking if I wanted to shoot their winter campaign.
And honestly I thought it was spam at first, because who emails a guy with a tripod that keeps falling over?
But it was real, and the brief was basically, take our new shell jacket to a glacier and make it look like the end of the world.
So they flew out two models, an art director named Kari, and me, and they are paying me to do the thing I would be doing anyway, which still feels illegal.
Kari sent over a mood board with like forty frames on it, mostly blue hour, lots of wind, people looking tiny against huge ice.
My job is to deliver twenty finished stills and a short vertical cut for their social team, by Friday.
Right, so let's talk about how you even plan a shoot like this.
The glacier we are going to is Sólheimajökull, and you cannot just walk onto it.
You need a guide, crampons, a helmet, the whole thing.
Our guide is called Siggi and he has already told me twice that if I step where he hasn't stepped, he is leaving me there.
I believe him.
For lenses I brought a thirty-five and an eighty-five, and that's it.
I know, I know, people are going to say, where's the zoom?
But on ice, with gloves on, swapping lenses is a nightmare, so I want as few decisions as possible.
Okay, day one.
We are on the ice, and the light is doing that thing where it's flat and grey and kind of ugly.
Which is a problem, because the mood board is all dramatic blue.
So we waited.
And waited.
Siggi made us hot chocolate out of a thermos that I'm pretty sure is older than me.
And then around three o'clock the cloud broke just a little, and the whole glacier turned this insane electric blue.
I was screaming at the models to get on the ridge, and Kari was screaming at me to stop screaming.
Look at this frame though.
That's straight out of camera, I haven't touched it.
The jacket is this deep orange, and against the blue ice it just pops, which, okay, is exactly why they picked orange.
Now, here's where it went wrong.
On day two the wind picked up to something stupid, like sixty kilometres an hour.
My tripod went over, obviously, because it always does.
And one of my batteries just died in the cold, completely, not even a little bit of charge left.
So the lesson for anyone thinking about winter shoots is, keep your spare batteries inside your jacket, against your body.
I knew that.
I still didn't do it.
We lost about two hours to the wind, and then Siggi called it because a storm was coming in off the coast.
So did we get the twenty frames?
We got fourteen that I'm happy with, and Kari thinks we can fill the rest from the backup set we shot near the van.
I'm going to spend the next three nights editing in a guesthouse with very bad wifi.
And honestly, as stressful as it was, this is the most fun I have had with a camera in years.
The pressure of someone else's deadline makes you shoot differently.
You stop overthinking and you just go.
Anyway, in the next video I'm going back up there on my own, no models, no client, just to shoot the ice cave Siggi showed us on the way down.
That one is going to be ridiculous.
See you on the glacier.
